name: variants
title: Rule variants under evaluation
description: Alternative formulations of rules the audit found firing on human prose. Nothing here replaces anything: the originals still ship unchanged and these sit beside them, so the two can be measured against the same corpus. Every rule is off by default. Scores are in research/audit.md.

rules.name: Echo, aligned
rules.description: The shared run must sit at the same end of both sentences, head or tail, rather than floating anywhere in them. Simon's own example repeats a tail: is an object in the system.

hit: A shopping cart is an object in the system. A chat room is an object in the system. A user session is an object in the system.
miss: In this study, we investigate the relationship between skull morphology and diet. We implement an integrative approach combining geometric morphometrics with performance testing.
The first four of these papers focus on system performance differences. This perspective belongs to a broader set of ideologies.

rules.name: Echo, three or more
rules.description: The original rule, but requiring three consecutive echoing sentences instead of two. Two sentences sharing a phrase is common in formal prose; three is a pattern.

rules.name: Echo, aligned and structural
rules.description: Aligned, and the shared run must carry at least two closed-class words. A span of content words is a shared subject, not a shared shape: the person who died is what a document is about, while is an object in the system is a frame with the nouns swapped out.

rules.name: Echo, structural
rules.description: The tightest form: three or more sentences sharing a run of at least three closed-class words. Catches the canonical example and nothing in the audit corpus at all.

rules.name: Transition-word addiction
rules.description: Not one Moreover, but the habit. Sources put the tell at paragraph level: if every paragraph opens with a transition word, the text is probably machine-written. Counts paragraph-opening transitions per 1000 words instead of flagging each one.

rules.name: Question runs of three
rules.description: Three consecutive questions rather than two. An essayist setting up a topic asks two; a machine asks three and answers them itself.

hit: What is it? Who is it for? Why now? Nobody has said.
miss: Who are the speakers of AAE? How are they viewed by others?

rules.name: Negative parallelism, tightened
rules.description: The original also matches ordinary English, as in not only because performance differences impair the system. This version requires the two halves to be parallel noun phrases, which is what makes the construction rhetorical rather than plain.

hit: This is not just a tool, but a philosophy.
It was not merely a change but a reinvention.
miss: not only because performance differences impair system performance, but the effect is small
She did not only fund the building, she also chose the architect.

rules.name: Negative parallelism, minus subordinate clauses
rules.description: The original's real errors are the cases where not only negates a clause rather than a thing: not only because performance differences impair the system. Three of its five hits on human prose were humans using the construction properly, which no rule should suppress. This version removes only the subordinate-clause form.

hit: This is not just a tool, but a philosophy.

miss: not only because performance differences impair the system, but the effect is small
He did not run because it was raining, but he walked.
